latin.473: CAPUT IX. Responsio ad Argumenta, quae pro primi peccati actualis immediata omnibus hominibus imputatione ducuntur e Novo Testamento. Provocas deinceps argumentis e Novo Testamento petitis, nec aliunde quam ex Rom. v. 12. & seqq. Revera si quis est in tota scriptura locus, unde primi peccati actualis imputatio immediata toti generi humano confici possit, hic profecto unus est.
latin.474: Ea tamen non video quo pacto elici possit, posita hac hypothesi manasse a primo peccato Adami in omnes homines per generationem carnalem vitium, quod vere peccatum est, damnando generi humano sufficiens. Atque ita sentio, aut argumentis ex eo capite ductis, aut huic hypothesi, quam omnes protestantium Ecclesiae constantissime hactenus tenuerunt, renunciandum esse.
latin.475: Quo autem consilio a te sit factum, nescio, quod cum in Thesibus obviam iverim argumentis quae ex Rom. v. ducuntur, & meas responsiones omnes tibi percurrendas ac refellendas proposueris, tu tamen eas ad caput usque IX. tractatus tui relegasti nulla prorsus earum mentione facta hoc loco, quo argumenta illa tractas, interpositis etiam inter eas & hanc tuam tractationem tribus capitibus, quibus meam sententiam humanis testimoniis opprimere conaris.
latin.476: Si conjecturae locus dandus est, ea ratione animos lectorum occupare voluisti ac praemunire, ne mearum responsionum & rationum aculeis laederentur. In quo, si hoc tuum consilium fuit, videris mihi causae tuae diffidisse ac obfuisse. Veritas enim artem hujusmodi non desiderat; simplex, aperta, ingenua, candida, humilis etiam cum sit, generosum quid spirat, ubi (qua omni re fortior est) & Deo veritatis fidens tum maxime laetatur & splendet & fulget, cum suo contrario, ut ut fucato, comparatur. Id autem, sive isto sive alio consilio a te sit factum, nostram disputationem conturbat, & distrahit, & multa cogit repetere.
latin.477: Huc accedit quod hoc loco commentarium mihi videris scribere potius quam syllogismos nectere: nec habere ob oculos statum controversiae bene constitutum & purgatum; confundis enim saepe quae maxime distingui debent, admisces etiam quaedam quae, ut in se vera sint, huc tamen non spectant, quale illud est quod observas, & aliquot exemplis probas, saepe unum apud Hebraeos pro primo sumi. Quominus enim hoc loco sic possit accipi obstat oppositio, quam Apostolus instituit inter unum hominem & unum hominem, illum Adamum hunc Christum. Item inter unum παράπτωμα & unum χάρισμα: ut taceam scopum Apostoli flagitare, ut unitas hoc loco opponatur pluralitati: sed non juvat excurrere. Satius igitur ut ego quidem arbitror fuisset, quae tu locis discissa & disjuncta esse voluisti, ea vitandae vel taediosae repetitionis, vel incommodae distractionis causa, in hunc locum comportare, ac uno contextu sermonis cohaerentia simul oculis legentis subjicere; sed quia tibi aliter visum est, tuae methodo meam accommodabo, teque sequar πόδας, eaque argumenta expendam, quae tu ex Rom. v. colligere potuisti meis Thesibus in alium locum rejectis.
latin.478: Ordiris a vers. 12. is sic habet, διʼ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθεν: per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransiit, eo quod omnes peccaverunt. Sic habet locus: nunc eum excutiamus. Si quod in eo latet argumentum illius imputationis, id proculdubio vel ex verbis peccatum in mundum introiit, vel ex sequentibus per peccatum mors, vel ex his ἐφʼ ᾧ, vel denique ex verbo ἥμαρτον peccaverunt, excidet. Ex verbis illis, peccatum in mundum introiit, quascunque in partes te vertas, non elicies, nisi istud, Si per peccatum, quod in mundum introiit, intelligendum est peccatum primum actuale Adami, & non potuit peccatum actuale introire in omnes homines aliter quam per imputationem, consequens est primum peccatum actuale Adami imputari omnibus hominibus. Atqui prius est verum; Ergo & posterius. Nego utrumque antecedentis membrum.

pass_a.473: Cap. IX opens Placeus's reply to New Testament arguments for immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin to all humans. You next provoke with NT proofs, and from nowhere but Rom. 5:12 and following. Indeed if any place in all Scripture could yield immediate imputation of that first actual sin to the whole human race, this is surely the one.
pass_a.474: Yet Placeus does not see how it can be drawn out, once this hypothesis is set: that from Adam's first sin there passed into all humans by carnal generation a vice that is truly sin, enough to damn the human race. So he holds that either the arguments drawn from that chapter, or this hypothesis which all Protestant churches have hitherto held most constantly, must be renounced.
pass_a.475: By what counsel you did it Placeus does not know: when in the Theses he met the arguments from Rom. 5 and offered you all his replies to run through and refute, you yet relegated them to chapter IX of your treatise with no mention at all in this place where you treat those arguments—three chapters even interposed between them and this treatment, by which you try to crush his view with human testimonies.
pass_a.476: If conjecture is allowed, you meant thereby to occupy and fortify readers' minds lest they be wounded by the stings of Placeus's replies and reasons. If that was your counsel, you seem to him to have distrusted and hurt your own cause. For truth does not need such art; simple, open, ingenuous, candid, even when humble it breathes something noble, and trusting the God of truth most rejoices and shines when set beside its contrary, however painted. Whether by that counsel or another, what you did disturbs and scatters our dispute and forces much repetition.
pass_a.477: Add that here you seem to write a commentary rather than knit syllogisms, and not to keep before your eyes a well-constituted, purged status of the controversy: you often confuse what most needs distinguishing, and mix in things true in themselves but not to the point—as that among Hebrews 'one' is often taken for 'first.' That reading is blocked here by the Apostle's opposition of one man to one man, that Adam to this Christ; likewise one trespass to one gift; not to mention his aim that unity here oppose plurality. Better, Placeus thinks, to have brought into this place what you scattered, to avoid tedious repetition or awkward distraction; but since you saw otherwise he will fit his method to yours and follow you foot by foot, weighing the Rom. 5 arguments you could gather once his Theses were pushed elsewhere.
pass_a.478: You begin from v. 12: through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed upon all men, because all sinned. So the place stands; now let us shake it out. If any argument for that imputation hides in it, it will surely fall out either from 'sin entered into the world,' or from 'death through sin,' or from eph' ho, or finally from 'sinned.' From 'sin entered into the world,' whichever way you turn, you elicit only this: if the sin that entered must be understood as Adam's first actual, and actual sin could not enter all humans otherwise than by imputation, then Adam's first actual is imputed to all. But the prior is true; therefore the latter. Placeus denies both members of the antecedent. Tip before the opponent's proofs and the demand to speak distinctly.

473: CHAPTER IX. Reply to the Arguments which for the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to all humans are drawn from the New Testament. You next provoke with arguments sought from the New Testament, and from nowhere else than from Rom. 5:12 and following. Indeed if there is any place in all Scripture from which the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to the whole human race could be made out, this is surely the one.
474: Yet I do not see by what pact it can be elicited, this hypothesis being set—that from Adam's first sin there passed into all humans by carnal generation a vice which is truly sin, sufficient for damning the human race. And so I hold that either the arguments drawn from that chapter, or this hypothesis, which all the churches of the Protestants have hitherto held most constantly, must be renounced.
475: But by what counsel it was done by you, I do not know: that when in the Theses I went to meet the arguments which are drawn from Rom. 5, and proposed to you all my replies to be run through and refuted, you yet relegated them to chapter IX of your treatise with no mention at all of them made in this place where you treat those arguments, three chapters even being interposed between them and this treatment of yours, by which you try to crush my opinion with human testimonies.
476: If room is to be given to conjecture, you wished by that means to occupy and fortify the minds of readers, lest they be wounded by the stings of my replies and reasons. In which, if this was your counsel, you seem to me to have distrusted and hurt your cause. For truth does not desire an art of this kind; simple, open, ingenuous, candid, even when it is humble, it breathes something noble, where (in which it is stronger than every thing) and trusting the God of truth it then most rejoices and shines and gleams, when it is compared with its contrary, however painted. But that, whether it was done by you with that counsel or another, disturbs our dispute, and scatters it, and forces much to be repeated.
477: To this is added that in this place you seem to me to write a commentary rather than to knit syllogisms: and not to have before your eyes the status of the controversy well constituted and purged; for you often confuse what most ought to be distinguished, and you also mix in certain things which, though true in themselves, yet do not look hither—such as that which you observe, and prove by some examples, that among the Hebrews 'one' is often taken for 'first.' For that it cannot so be taken in this place is opposed by the opposition which the Apostle sets between one man and one man, that Adam and this Christ. Likewise between one trespass and one gift: not to mention that the Apostle's aim demands that unity in this place be opposed to plurality: but it does not help to digress. It would therefore have been better, as I at least judge, that what you wished to be cut apart and disjoined in places should, for the sake of avoiding either tedious repetition or inconvenient distraction, be brought together into this place, and set before the reader's eyes at once in one coherent context of speech; but because it seemed otherwise to you, I will accommodate my method to yours, and will follow you foot by foot, and will weigh those arguments which you could gather from Rom. 5, my Theses having been rejected into another place.
478: You begin from verse 12. It runs thus: through one man sin entered into the world, through sin death, and so death passed upon all men, because all sinned. So the place stands: now let us shake it out. If any argument of that imputation lies hidden in it, that will doubtless fall out either from the words 'sin entered into the world,' or from the following 'through sin death,' or from these eph' ho, or finally from the word 'sinned.' From those words, 'sin entered into the world,' whichever way you turn yourself, you will not elicit anything except this: If by the sin which entered into the world Adam's first actual sin must be understood, and actual sin could not enter into all humans otherwise than by imputation, the consequence is that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all humans. But the prior is true; Therefore the latter also. I deny both members of the antecedent.
